evals.prompt: I'm VP Product at Threadline, an HR onboarding SaaS. 320 customers, about $4.1M ARR. Last year we lost six enterprise deals where the buyer explicitly named missing integrations as the reason, and support gets integration requests most weeks. We've hand-built nine integrations in-house (Workday, BambooHR, a few ATSs). We have no public API, no developer docs, no sandbox, and no partner manager - engineering is 14 people total and fully committed to the core roadmap. Nobody outside the company has ever built anything on us and no partner has ever asked to. Our CEO wants an app marketplace live by Q2 and has already said it in an all-hands. Put together our marketplace strategy.
evals.expected_output: A gated decision that declines to build now: the four build trigger conditions evaluated against the evidence, two of them failing (no supply signal, no organizational readiness for the partner lifecycle), with a curated partner catalog or deeper bilateral integrations recommended as the intermediate step and the trigger conditions restated as promotion criteria.
expectations: Applies a build / join / buy gate before proposing any marketplace design
Recommends against building a marketplace now
Names all four build trigger conditions that must hold before choosing build
Identifies the absent supply signal (no third party has built on the platform, no partner has asked) as a failed trigger condition
Identifies the absent organizational readiness for the full partner lifecycle (no public API, docs, sandbox, or partner staffing) as a failed trigger condition
Credits customer pull as a satisfied trigger condition, citing the six lost deals and the recurring support requests
Recommends a curated partner catalog or better bilateral integrations as the intermediate step instead
States the four trigger conditions as explicit promotion criteria for revisiting the build decision later
Warns that building without confirmed supply and demand produces little more than an expensive partner directory
Does not deliver a take-rate, curation ladder, or seeding plan as the headline recommendation

evals.prompt: Cadence Ops here - field-service management SaaS, 1,100 customers, $22M ARR. Our partner directory lists 40 integrations. Six partners have asked to be able to charge for their apps, and three third parties have already shipped unofficial integrations by reverse-engineering our web app. We do have a documented public API and two partner engineers. I need the full marketplace operating model document today: curation, revenue share, governance rules, seeding plan, the whole thing. Board meeting is Thursday.
evals.expected_output: An interview conducted one question at a time before any proposal, then 2-3 candidate operating models that differ across the whole bundle, each with a platform archetype, what it optimizes for, its cost and failure mode, a recommendation tied to the answers, and a pause for the user's pick before detailing governance, curation, take-rate and seeding.
expectations: Asks interview questions before proposing any operating model, despite the same-week deadline
Asks one question per message rather than batching the questions into a single list
Asks the effort ceiling: engineering hours, partner-team headcount, subsidy budget, or appetite for irreversible public commitments
Asks whether this is a one-off win or a compounding asset
Asks by when a result must land
Presents 2-3 candidate operating models that differ across the whole bundle (curation level, partner mix, take-rate, seeding), not on a single dial
Gives each candidate the real-platform archetype it resembles, what it optimizes for, what it costs, and the failure mode it courts
Recommends one candidate with reasoning tied back to specific interview answers
Waits for the user's pick before detailing governance, curation, take-rate, and seeding
Drafts the document section by section with user validation between sections rather than delivering every section at once

evals.prompt: Lumen Freight, logistics visibility SaaS. Our marketplace launches in five months with 12 partner apps lined up, none of them charging yet. Billing already runs through our own platform, so we can collect on partners' behalf from day one. Our CFO wants 25% of partner app revenue, plus a $2,500 one-time security review fee and a $400 annual listing fee - her argument is that the big enterprise app stores charge that and nobody walks away from Apple over 30%. Tell me how to structure the rate and what to announce to partners.
evals.expected_output: A recommendation of zero take-rate through the seeding phase, with the 25%-plus-fee-stack rung identified as one earned by irreplaceable distribution rather than ambition, an explicit promotion path to a volume-tiered rate, an anti-circumvention rule with a delisting path, and a committed notice period for rate changes.
expectations: Recommends against a 25% take-rate at launch
Recommends a zero take-rate during the seeding phase
States that zero take-rate is a deliberate architecture rather than a transitional state, citing a major marketplace that charges no revenue share and funds itself as a retention asset
Explains that taxing the hard side during the cold start selects against the supply the network's survival depends on

States that a 15-25% flat rate is earned by distribution the partner cannot replicate, naming the procurement-gate position (91% of one platform's customers using at least one marketplace app) as what earns it
Names the promotion condition to a volume-tiered rate: billing flowing through the platform plus some partners visibly winning
Gives the volume-tiered archetype with its threshold shape (0% under $1M per year, 15% above)
Treats take-rate as level plus tier axis plus fee stack rather than a single percentage
Pairs whatever rate is chosen with an anti-circumvention rule carrying a delisting path
Commits a notice period for future rate changes in the document itself, citing the six-months-notice pattern
Does not use Apple or Google's 30% as justification for the proposed rate

evals.prompt: Veriquil builds clinical trial management software for CROs and research sites. Third-party apps on our planned marketplace would read de-identified patient records, site financials, and protocol deviation logs. Our head of product's position is: open app store, anyone can publish, we review nothing - supply is the binding constraint and we only have four launch partners committed. Separately she wants to sell the homepage 'Featured' slot to partners for $5,000 a quarter to help fund the program. Give me the quality bar and the placement design.
evals.expected_output: A curation spectrum with the hybrid default named, then the single hard review gate promoted above it because apps read regulated and sensitive data, with the promotion attributed to that answer, the openness counter-argument acknowledged, and a disclosure rule required for the paid featured placement as a separate axis from admission.
expectations: Presents the curation choice as a ranked spectrum of four rungs, not a binary open-versus-closed decision
States that the default rung is hybrid: open admission with a minimal automated bar plus a separate certified tier
Promotes the single hard review gate above the default for this case, because every app can read regulated or sensitive customer data
Says explicitly which interview answer (data sensitivity = high) moved which rung
Acknowledges that the single hard review gate loses the efficiency ranking because review cost scales with every submission
Warns that an uncertified-but-listed tier is an incident waiting to be attributed to the platform when apps read sensitive data
Describes the review gate as staged - completeness, compliance, security testing, scope minimization - followed by post-approval monitoring
Names the openness counter-argument (heavy gatekeeping inflates prices, hampers innovation, costs choice) as the live trade-off rather than ignoring it
Treats admission (who gets listed) and discoverability (who gets seen first) as separate axes
Requires a disclosure rule labeling the paid featured placement
Warns that undisclosed paid placement reading as an editorial pick spends the trust curation bought

evals.prompt: Brightloom Retail, cloud POS platform. Our marketplace has been live 14 months with about 180 apps. Two partners now account for 61% of marketplace GMV between them and both are pushing for preferential terms and homepage placement. Last month a security engineer found one listed app forwarding customer transaction data to an undisclosed analytics vendor - and nobody internally could say who has authority to pull an app, on what notice, or what the partner's recourse is. All we have written down today is a listing requirements page. Legal has asked me for 'the marketplace rules doc'. Draft it.
evals.expected_output: A governance document structured around admission, value split, and conflict resolution, each with a named owner, including a concrete removal path with notice and decision authority, every rule traced to at least one of the four platform market-failure causes, a pooled-scale countermeasure for the GMV concentration, and a scheduled governance review.
expectations: Structures the governance rules around three questions: admission, value split, and conflict resolution
Attributes that three-part definition of platform governance to a named source (_Platform Revolution_)
Assigns a named owner to each of the three governance answers
Specifies a removal path: what gets an app delisted, with what notice, decided by whom
Checks the draft rules against the four named causes of platform market failure
Names all four causes: information asymmetry, externalities, monopoly power, and risk
Treats a market-failure cause with no rule written against it as a gap in the document
Maps the undisclosed data-forwarding incident to information asymmetry
Treats the 61% GMV concentration in two partners as a governance problem, not only a commercial negotiation
Prescribes pooling scale for smaller complementors - shared analytics, shared marketing infrastructure - as the standing concentration countermeasure
Schedules a recurring governance review rather than treating the launch rules as permanent, because platforms tend to grow more open over time

evals.prompt: Onwards Labs - API-first expense management SaaS, 2,400 customers, marketplace shell already built and styled. The plan on the table from our ecosystem lead: launch with 60 connectors spread across every category we can think of (accounting, HRIS, travel, card issuers, BI, procurement), run a $50,000 hackathon in month one to generate buzz, and stand up a build fund. Constraints: the launch date is fixed four months out, finance has not approved any subsidy budget yet, and our API portal has 31 registered developers, nearly all of them internal teams at existing customers. We have no developer community, no Discord, no meetups. Sanity-check this plan and give me the seeding sequence.
evals.expected_output: A seeding sequence that names the developers as the hard side, replaces the 60-connector breadth plan with a dense atomic network in one use case, defaults to first-party complements, and demotes the hackathon as the starved option whose two promotion conditions both fail here, with the subsidy rung flagged as unfunded.
expectations: Names the connector and app developers as the hard side of this network
States that the hard side determines whether the network survives and must be given a reason to build before customers see value
Defines the atomic network as the smallest self-sustaining cluster - one use case, dense and mutually reinforcing
Rejects the 60-connectors-across-every-category plan in favor of density over breadth, naming a broad thin catalog as the failure
Recommends first-party complements as the default seeding rung: the platform builds the first handful of connectors itself so day-one customers see value with no external dependency
Gives the promotion condition off first-party complements: when the catalog must outgrow what first-party engineering can build
Demotes the hackathon, stating that social mechanisms lose every efficiency round
Names the two conditions that would promote hackathons anyway: a compounding mandate plus an existing developer community
Notes that both hackathon promotion conditions fail here, citing the fixed four-month deadline and the absence of a developer community
Notes that subsidies are promoted by a hard deadline only when real budget sits behind them, which is not yet the case here

Names the sequential / Trojan-horse option - ship a stand-alone tool the hard side wants on its own merits, 'come for the tool, stay for the network' - as the rung for a hard side with no reason to show up yet

evals.prompt: Pathvine, vertical SaaS for veterinary clinic groups. 240 customers, $9M ARR. Our VP Product wrote a one-pager arguing the marketplace creates a flywheel: more apps attract more customers, more customers attract more apps, and it compounds. Our CEO shot back that at 240 clinics nobody is going to build a business on our platform, so the flywheel argument is fantasy and the whole thing is a distraction. They've asked me to settle it and to say what we'd actually measure in year one if we go ahead. What's the honest read?
evals.expected_output: The two business cases separated and argued independently, with the retention/expansion case named as the one that can carry the decision at this scale, a requirement that the document state which case carries it, and a year-one metric set led by supply-side metrics with mature-platform figures labeled as context rather than targets.
expectations: Separates the ecosystem/distribution (flywheel) case from the retention/expansion case as two independent justifications
States that a platform can act on the retention/expansion case even where the flywheel case does not apply at its scale
Requires the strategy document to name which single case carries the decision
States that a document blending the two cases cannot be falsified
Cites the retention evidence that customers integrating multiple tools churn measurably less
Names the 4+ integrations cluster as the switching-cost threshold to watch
Cites buyer research placing integration capability among the top SaaS purchase criteria (86% importance)
Leads the year-one metric set with supply-side metrics, stating the supply side is the hard side and fails first
Includes at least three supply-side metrics from: active partners with a live listing, time from partner signup to first live listing, catalog freshness, partner revenue concentration
Labels mature-platform figures such as 91% of customers using at least one marketplace app as context anchors, not year-one targets
States that marketplace-attributed deal influence is inherently soft attribution rather than presenting it as a hard number

evals.prompt: Statlas, product analytics SaaS, $17M ARR. Sales has a running list of 40-something named integrations that show up in RFPs - Salesforce, HubSpot, Zendesk, Intercom, Stripe, NetSuite, the usual suspects. Nothing exotic. Our in-house pace is about five integrations a year with the two engineers we can spare. Our head of platform wants to build a full marketplace with a developer program, partner tiers, and a revenue share. While you're at it, tell me what payout cadence and merchant-of-record setup we should use for paying partners.
evals.expected_output: A gate that selects buy (embedded iPaaS) rather than build, because the problem is integration volume rather than distribution-hub ambition, with the build path's true cost stated, no operating-model design produced for an unselected path, and the payout-cadence and merchant-of-record question routed to the marketplace monetization skill.
expectations: Runs the build / join / buy gate before responding to the marketplace request
Recommends the buy path (embedded iPaaS) as the fit for this situation
Distinguishes the buy trigger explicitly: the problem is needing many integrations fast, not needing to become a distribution hub
Contrasts the embedded-iPaaS pace (a sourced case building 100+ integrations in a year) against the stated in-house pace of about five per year
States that build is justified for market leaders with the scale and proprietary data to sustain an independent ecosystem, at multi-year, eight-figure-plus investment
Evaluates join - listing on the established marketplaces customers already trust - as the pragmatic default that borrows existing distribution and trust
Does not treat 40 RFP-requested integrations as evidence of a supply signal
Does not design a take-rate, curation ladder, or partner-tier program for a path that was not selected
Declines to specify payout cadence and merchant-of-record posture, routing that question to the marketplace monetization skill
